fact_text: Foreign nationals and overseas Koreans who reside in Korea and work at an insured company are compulsorily enrolled in the National Health Insurance as employee insured; enrolment can be excluded only if equivalent medical coverage is proven under a foreign law, foreign insurance, or an employer contract.
evidence_quote: Foreigners and overseas Koreans residing and working at the insured company are compulsorily subscribed.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a corporate private or international health plan lets you skip Korea's state scheme. Actually enrolment in the National Health Insurance is compulsory for foreign employees, with an opt-out only where equivalent cover is proven. Action: budget for NHIS payroll deductions from your first pay run and seek exclusion only with documented equivalent coverage.

entity_title: 6-month rule: mandatory NHIS for foreign residents
fact_text: Any foreigner or overseas Korean who has stayed in Korea for more than six months is subject to mandatory subscription to National Health Insurance as self-employed (locally) insured if not already covered as an employee, which also captures non-working accompanying family.
evidence_quote: Any foreigner or overseas Korean who has stayed in Korea for over six months is subject to mandatory subscription to health insurance(From July 16, 2019)

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a non-working spouse or dependant can remain uninsured. Actually a foreigner staying over six months is mandatorily enrolled and billed premiums. Action: register accompanying family with NHIS and plan for their premium bills once past six months of stay.

entity_title: NHIS premiums split 50/50 with the employer
fact_text: For the employee insured, the monthly National Health Insurance contribution equals monthly wage times the contribution rate and is paid half by the employee (withheld from salary) and half by the employer.
evidence_quote: Contribution is paid by the employee insured (50%) and the employer (50%).

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the employer or the state fully funds Korean health cover. Actually the premium is split 50/50 and the employee's half is deducted from salary each month. Action: model roughly half of the NHIS premium as a recurring payroll deduction when estimating net pay.

entity_title: Changing or adding a workplace needs prior immigration permission
fact_text: A foreign worker who wants to change or add a workplace, even within the scope permitted by their visa status, must obtain immigration permission in advance (and, where only reporting applies, report within 15 days); doing so without permission is an Immigration Act violation.
evidence_quote: For a foreign worker to change or add the workplace within the scope permitted under the visa status, that person is required to obtain permission in advance

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed that once you hold a Korean work visa you can switch employers like a local hire. Actually a work visa is tied to an approved workplace and you must get immigration permission before changing or adding one. Action: secure the workplace-change permit before starting at any new employer, not after signing.

fact_text: A foreigner intending to stay in Korea for 90 days or more must apply for foreign resident registration (Alien Registration Card) within 90 days of entry; failing to register is an Immigration Act violation carrying a fine.
evidence_quote: to apply for foreign resident registration within 90 days of entry

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the entry visa is enough to live and transact in Korea. Actually you must obtain the Alien Registration Card (foreign resident registration) within 90 days of entry, and it is what unlocks banking, phone and most services. Action: book the immigration-office reservation and register well inside the 90-day window.

entity_title: Re-entry permit exemption lapses after one year abroad
fact_text: Registered foreign residents are exempt from obtaining a re-entry permit and may re-enter Korea within one year of departure (within their authorized stay); staying abroad beyond that without a re-entry permit jeopardises the resident status.
evidence_quote: Registered foreigners who would depart after April 1, 2022 will be exempt from the Re-entry Permit and allowed re-entry into the Republic of Korea within 1 year from the date of departure

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a valid residence card means you can leave and return any time while it is valid. Actually the re-entry exemption only covers absences up to one year; a longer absence needs a re-entry permit obtained before leaving or the status can lapse. Action: if a trip abroad will exceed one year, apply for a re-entry permit before departure.

entity_title: Report a change of address within 15 days
fact_text: A registered foreign resident who moves must report the change of residence to a community service center or immigration office within 15 days of moving in (14 days for F-4 holders).
evidence_quote: The change must be reported within 15 days from the date of move in for registered foreign residents and within 14 days from the date of move in for F-4 visa holders.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the housing lease and its registration are a purely private matter. Actually every change of residence must be reported to immigration or the local office within 15 days, and the address on file drives official mail and benefits. Action: report your new address within 15 days of moving, bringing passport, residence card and proof of residence.

fact_text: A foreign employee may elect a 19% flat tax rate on gross wage and salary instead of Korea's progressive rates; under the flat rate, non-taxable income is included and deductions, exemptions and tax credits cannot be applied.
evidence_quote: Under the flat tax rate, the amount of tax is calculated by multiplying 19% to the gross wage & salary.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the 19% flat rate is automatically the cheaper option for foreign workers. Actually electing it means losing all deductions, exemptions and tax credits and taxing otherwise non-taxable income, so it only wins at higher salaries. Action: compute tax both ways (flat vs progressive) before electing, and file the flat-rate application to claim it.

entity_title: Korean tax residents are taxed on worldwide income
fact_text: Under the Income Tax Act, a Korean tax resident is liable to tax on worldwide income, whereas a non-resident is taxed only on Korea-source income.
evidence_quote: A resident is obligated to pay tax in Korea for worldwide income, and a non-resident is obligated to pay tax only for domestic source income.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed only your Korean salary is taxable in Korea. Actually once you are a Korean tax resident your worldwide income is in scope (subject to treaty relief and foreign tax credit). Action: map all non-Korean income and any tax-treaty position before your first Korean filing.

entity_title: Tax residency turns on 183 days, not nationality
fact_text: For income-tax purposes a resident is, in principle, an individual with a domicile in Korea or a place of residence in Korea for 183 days or longer; residency is decided on these facts, not on nationality or holding permanent residency.
evidence_quote: In principle, a resident refers to an individual who has had his/her domicile in Korea or a place of residence in Korea for 183 days or longer.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you stay a non-resident (foreign) taxpayer as long as you keep foreign citizenship. Actually residency turns on domicile or 183 days of residence in Korea, and NTS states it is not determined by nationality or permanent residency. Action: track your days and centre-of-life factors, since crossing into residency changes your entire tax base.
